items.headline: FinCEN proposes changes to beneficial ownership verification and risk-based CDD
items.what_happened: FinCEN announced a proposed rule amending the Customer Due Diligence Rule on 17 November 2026. The proposal was published in the Federal Register on 19 November 2026 as document 2026-23614 (91 FR 74514), with comments due by 19 January 2027. FinCEN describes three targeted revisions to 31 CFR 1010.230. First, the proposed text would make explicit that, where warranted by other risk indicators or supervisory concerns, a covered financial institution may obtain additional information, including information relevant to lawful immigration status and employment authorization in the United States. Second, it would codify the February 2026 exceptive relief (FIN-2026-R001), so that beneficial owners of a legal entity customer are identified when the customer first opens an account, when the institution has knowledge of facts that would reasonably call into question the reliability of information previously obtained, and as needed under its risk-based ongoing due diligence procedures. Third, it would move the list of beneficial owner information into the rule text and provide that an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number is not an acceptable identifying number for a beneficial owner. FinCEN proposes that the rule take effect 90 days after publication of a final rule in the Federal Register.
items.why_it_matters: This is a proposed rule, not a current legal requirement. It does not abolish beneficial ownership identification or verification. The February 2026 relief already exists, and the November proposal would formalise it and add other changes. The additional information provision is permissive (the institution may obtain it where risk indicators or supervisory concerns warrant) and does not make immigration status or employment authorization information a universal mandatory check.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Map how onboarding, beneficial ownership verification and ongoing monitoring controls distinguish new customers, existing customers opening further accounts, information whose reliability is in question and risk-triggered refreshes. Assess the proposed information collection and additional enquiry provisions separately, and do not implement them as current legal requirements before a final rule.

items.headline: EU expands Russia sanctions across financial institutions and energy networks
items.what_happened: On 16 November 2026 the Council of the EU announced additional restrictive measures on 12 individuals and 101 entities. The Council said the listings include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, individuals associated with Wildberries and Ozon, additional entities and businesspersons in the Russian oil and energy sector, and companies from the United Arab Emirates, China, Seychelles and Oman that it described as buyers of crude oil products of Russian origin, together with businesspersons who own or manage vessels subject to EU restrictive measures. The implementing regulation identifies Tatyana Kim as founder and CEO of Wildberries, and Alexander Chachava as the owner of a holding company described as holding the largest share in Ozon. The listings were adopted under the EU framework on actions undermining or threatening Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence, through Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2575 and Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2574. The Council said those listed are subject to an asset freeze and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available to them, and that a travel ban applies to the natural persons.
items.why_it_matters: The total of 113 is made up of individuals and entities, not 113 banks or vessels, and the Council gives the bank figure only as nearly 50. The Council announcement summarises the package. The listing annexes to the two legal acts identify the persons and entities and fix the measures. These are asset freeze listings, so they should not be described as a general prohibition on dealing with every Russian bank or as new vessel designations. Where the Council refers to businesspersons who own or manage vessels, the listing attaches to those persons, not automatically to the ships.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Reconcile the new entries against EU sanctions data from the annexes to Decision 2026/2575 and Implementing Regulation 2026/2574, then test exposure through banking counterparties, commodity trading relationships, corporate ownership and control, and maritime intermediaries. Record the legal basis for each match rather than relying on the press summary.

items.headline: OFAC targets cyber scam operators and armed group facilitators in Southeast Asia
items.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 the US Treasury announced that OFAC had sanctioned three individuals and two affiliated companies in connection with cyber scam centers in Southeast Asia, under E.O. 13694, as further amended. Treasury said Zhao Hui, a Cambodian national, leased a scam center owned by an OFAC designated person and paid protection fees to the OFAC designated leader of the Prince Group TCO, and also owned a scam compound in Cambodia that Treasury said primarily targeted Americans and Europeans through virtual currency investment scams. Treasury designated two Cambodia based companies, Bei Fang Bo Lin Construction Decoration Co., Ltd and ZHZ Investment Consulting Co., Ltd., as owned or controlled by, or acting for or on behalf of, Zhao. Treasury also designated Saw Shwe Wah, which it described as commander in chief of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), and Saw A One, a DKBA commander, as leaders or officials of the DKBA, which was previously designated by OFAC.
items.why_it_matters: This is a sanctions designation announcement and the descriptions of conduct are Treasury’s assessments, not criminal convictions. The action reaches both a compound operator and companies tied to him, and armed group figures whose designation rests on their roles in an already designated group. Treasury states that the property of designated persons in the United States or in the possession or control of US persons is blocked, and that entities owned 50 percent or more, directly or indirectly and in the aggregate, by blocked persons are also blocked.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Update screening from the authoritative OFAC SDN entries, check aliases, identifiers and programme tags, and apply ownership rules to customers and counterparties. Escalate on specific evidence connecting a customer or transaction to a designated person, such as company control, compound leasing or protection payments, rather than on geography or sector alone.

items.headline: SFO charges eight in London Capital & Finance fraud investigation
items.what_happened: On 16 November 2026 the Serious Fraud Office announced that it had charged eight individuals following its investigation into the collapse of London Capital & Finance Plc, which collapsed in 2019. The SFO said that more than 11,200 investors lost an estimated £251 million. According to the SFO, six defendants are charged with conspiracy to defraud, one with concealing criminal property, and an eighth with conspiracy to defraud and acting in contravention of a director disqualification undertaking. The SFO said all eight defendants are due to appear before Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 7 December, and that it understood the eighth defendant’s legal team will apply for anonymity at the first hearing.
items.why_it_matters: A charge is an allegation. It does not establish guilt, and the defendants should not be described as convicted. The £251 million is the SFO’s estimate of investor losses arising from the firm’s collapse, not a finding that each loss is a proven criminal loss attributable to a particular defendant. The case is a milestone in a long running investigation, and it separates the proof needed for criminal liability from earlier questions about detection and regulatory oversight.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Keep separate the detection of suspicious investment activity, the tracing of investor funds, any regulatory shortcomings and the evidence needed to prove criminal liability. Use the charges as a reference point for typology review, not as established findings.

items.headline: European Commission creates central EU Sanctions Office
items.what_happened: The European Commission announced the creation of an EU Sanctions Office to bring together its expertise across the sanctions lifecycle, from policy design to implementation, enforcement and anti-circumvention, including engagement with third countries. The Commission said the Office will sit within the Secretariat-General under the political responsibility of Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque. It also appointed Lars Danielsson as International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions, taking up the position on 6 February 2027 when the mandate of the current Envoy ends. The Commission said these changes take effect on 16 January 2027. The Commission published the original press release, IP/26/2499, on 18 November 2026. The European Commission Representation in Cyprus republished it on 19 November 2026.
items.why_it_matters: This is an institutional change within the Commission. It is not a new sanctions regulation and does not add prohibitions or compliance duties for businesses. The Commission said the Office will support Member States with faster compliance guidance, data sharing and economic and technical analysis, so future guidance and coordination are the points to watch.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Monitor guidance and coordination from the new Office, particularly on third country circumvention, shipping intermediaries, financial channels and complex ownership structures, and do not treat the announcement itself as creating new obligations.

supporting_sources.note: Republication of IP/26/2499 by the Commission Representation in Cyprus, 19 November 2026
